newsitem.title: USA: Iranian exiles urge G7 to boycott Tehran.
newsitem.headline: Iranian exiles urge G7 to boycott Tehran.

text.p: Hundreds of Iranian exiles marched through Denver on Friday, demanding that the Group of Seven summit here impose an economic, political and military boycott on the clerical government in Tehran.

Banging drums and cymbals, waving lighted torches as a symbol of freedom, they processed under escort by mounted police from Denver's state Capitol to a point one block from the public library where the summit was to open hours later.

"No trade, no ties, no arms to the mullahs," chanted the protesters, estimated by police to number between 1,200 and 1,500. The National Council of Resistance of Iran (NCR), which organised the march, said 6,000 to 7,000 people took part.
Iran, listed as one of the summit topics, is a divisive subject among participants, most of which have refused to follow the tough line taken by the United States.

The European Union in April dropped its "critical dialogue" with Iran and withdrew ambassadors after a German court found that Tehran leaders had plotted the murder of exiles in Berlin, but the EU has not imposed trade sanctions like Washington.

A resolution adopted by the marchers called on the G7 to "refer the clerical regime's export of terrorism and abuse of human rights to the United Nations Security Council" and hand over Iran's U.N. seat to the NCR.

At a rally earlier outside the gold-domed Capitol, the Colorado state legislature, U.S. Democratic Representative Gary Ackerman of New York lent support to the demonstrators, saying continued tolerance of the Iranian government was unacceptable.
"It is time for the G7 to show its disgust with this reprehensible regime," he said to loud applause from spectators waving Iranian flags from before the 1979 Islamic Revolution.

The crowd watched on a video display a satellite hook-up with a rally at an NCR military base in Iraq, close to the Iranian border, addressed by the husband-and-wife leaders of the grouping, Massoud and Maryam Rajavi.

The officials said their march was the only one that Denver city authorities had permitted during the G7 summit, which continues until Sunday. The United States, Britain, France, Germany, Italy, Canada and Japan are G7 members and Russia is also attending the gathering.

Despite strong antipathy to Tehran for its alleged support of terrorism, hostility to Middle East peace and pursuit of weapons of mass destruction, the U.S. government does not support the NCR, the leading Iranian resistance organisation.

U.S. officials say the group has an anti-American past, engages in acts of terrorism in Iran and is heavily dependent on Iraq, which Washington considers no better than Iran. The NCR denies this, saying it pursues democratic goals.

The NCR says it is a coalition of Iranian opposition groups but grew out of the People's Mujahideen, an Islamic-cum-Marxist group that fought the former Shah and attempted to join the Islamic Revolution before being forced underground again.
